name: GRIN1-related neurodevelopmental disorder (NMDA receptor GluN1 encephalopathy)

clinicalPearls: GRIN1 encodes the obligatory GluN1 subunit present in every NMDA receptor, so pathogenic variants disturb glutamatergic signalling across virtually the whole brain, producing a severe, early-onset encephalopathy.
The core phenotype is profound global developmental delay with absent or minimal speech, severe intellectual disability and, in most, no independent walking.
Stereotypic hyperkinetic movements are a strong clue: oculogyric crises, dystonia, chorea, limb stereotypies and characteristic recurrent hand or arm movements.
Cortical visual impairment is frequent, with poor fixation and roving eye movements out of proportion to any structural ocular abnormality.
Most children have muscular hypotonia of central origin, often with superimposed spasticity, plus feeding difficulty and disturbed sleep.

Both dominant de novo missense variants (often gain- or loss-of-function affecting channel gating) and biallelic loss-of-function variants occur; the recessive form tends to be particularly severe with early cortical visual impairment.
Epilepsy affects many but not all patients and ranges from infantile spasms to focal and generalised seizures; a subset has an epileptic encephalopathy pattern.
Acquired microcephaly and progressive brain atrophy on imaging are common, distinguishing it from purely static encephalopathies.
reference.pathophysiology: The disorder is caused by pathogenic variants in GRIN1, which encodes GluN1 (NR1), the mandatory glycine-binding subunit that assembles with GluN2 subunits to form functional N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptors. Because GluN1 is a constituent of every NMDA receptor, its dysfunction has pervasive effects on excitatory neurotransmission, synaptic plasticity and neuronal development. Dominant de novo missense variants typically cluster in the transmembrane and linker domains that govern channel gating, agonist potency and magnesium block; functionally these behave as gain-of-function (increased current, reduced magnesium sensitivity or heightened agonist potency) or as dominant-negative loss-of-function, and the direction of the functional change has therapeutic implications. Biallelic loss-of-function (null) variants abolish or severely reduce receptor availability and produce a recessive, often more uniformly severe encephalopathy. The resulting imbalance between excitation and inhibition during critical developmental windows underlies the developmental delay, movement disorder, cortical visual impairment and, in many, seizures, and correlates with the acquired microcephaly and cerebral atrophy seen radiologically.
additionalDifferentials: GRIN2A- and GRIN2B-related neurodevelopmental disorders and epileptic encephalopathies (sibling NMDA-receptor subunit disorders)
FOXG1 syndrome and other Rett-like encephalopathies
Non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia (glycine encephalopathy) and other neurometabolic encephalopathies
Anti-NMDA-receptor autoimmune encephalitis (acquired mimic of the movement and behavioural features)
additionalInvestigations: Trio exome or genome sequencing (diagnostic gold standard; confirms de novo dominant versus biallelic recessive inheritance)
Targeted epileptic-encephalopathy or neurodevelopmental gene panel including the GRIN family
Brain MRI looking for cerebral atrophy, delayed myelination, thin corpus callosum and acquired microcephaly
Electroencephalography, including extended or video EEG when an epileptic encephalopathy is suspected
Ophthalmology and visual electrophysiology to characterise cortical visual impairment
Functional electrophysiological characterisation of the variant (research setting) to classify gain- versus loss-of-function
Serial developmental, feeding and swallowing assessment
redFlags: New or worsening seizures, prolonged seizures or status epilepticus
Acute deterioration in tone, alertness or movement suggesting intercurrent illness or an alternative acquired cause such as autoimmune encephalitis
Progressive feeding difficulty with aspiration or failure to thrive
Deceleration of head growth and regression of previously acquired skills
Severe sleep disruption or autonomic instability affecting overall stability
reference.prognosis: GRIN1-related disorder is a lifelong, severe neurodevelopmental condition; most affected individuals have profound intellectual disability, limited or absent speech and significant motor disability, and the biallelic loss-of-function form is generally the most severe. Life expectancy is influenced by seizure burden, feeding safety and respiratory complications, and care is largely supportive and multidisciplinary.
pitfalls: Assuming the encephalopathy is static: acquired microcephaly and progressive atrophy can be mistaken for a fixed insult such as hypoxic-ischaemic injury.
Overlooking the diagnosis when seizures are absent, since epilepsy is not universal and the movement disorder and cortical visual impairment may dominate.
Failing to distinguish gain-of-function from loss-of-function variants, which matters because their theoretical pharmacological approaches differ.
Attributing the hyperkinetic movements or oculogyric episodes to seizures and escalating antiseizure medication inappropriately.
Missing the recessive form by stopping at a single heterozygous variant rather than confirming biallelic status on trio testing.
